notes.front: What is an atom?
notes.back: The most basic building block of all matter, made of three subatomic particles: protons, neutrons and electrons.
notes.explanation: The numbers of these three particles define each element, which is why hydrogen and helium behave differently.
notes.example: Like a single brick in a wall: the hydrogen atom, the simplest, has one proton in its nucleus and one orbiting electron.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Atom”, PDF p. 442
notes.evidence: The atom is considered to be the most basic building block of all matter. Atoms are composed of three subatomic particles: protons, neutrons, and electrons.

notes.front: What are valence electrons?
notes.back: The electrons in an atom’s outermost shell; they can take part in chemical bonds with other atoms.
notes.explanation: The number of electrons in the outermost shell is what decides the atom’s valence, so these electrons are named after it.
notes.example: Copper has one electron in its outer orbit: that lone outer electron is copper’s valence electron.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Valence Electrons”, PDF p. 443
notes.evidence: The number of electrons in the outermost shell of the atom is the determining factor in its valence. Therefore, the electrons contained in this shell are called valence electrons.

notes.front: What are free electrons?
notes.back: Loosely bound outermost electrons that are easily dislodged from the attraction of the protons in the nucleus.
notes.explanation: Being loosely bound and far from the nucleus, they are the electrons that can break away and move through a material.
notes.example: Like loose change in a pocket rather than coins sewn into the lining: at room temperature a silver wire has billions of them.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Free Electrons”, PDF p. 443
notes.evidence: These outermost electrons are called “free” electrons because they can be easily dislodged from the positive attraction of the protons in the nucleus.

notes.front: What is static electricity?
notes.back: A build-up of electrical charge on the surface of an object, with no current flowing.
notes.explanation: It is called static because the charge stays put instead of flowing as it does in a working circuit.
notes.example: Like a plastic rod rubbed with fur: the rod becomes negatively charged and the fur positively charged, yet nothing flows.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Static Electricity”, PDF p. 445
notes.evidence: Static electricity is a buildup of an electrical charge on the surface of an object.

notes.front: What is electrostatic discharge (ESD), and why does it matter to a technician?
notes.back: The discharge of static electricity, such as from the human body; it is one of the most frequent causes of damage to solid-state components.
notes.explanation: Simply handling a sensitive device can discharge the body’s static into it, so careless handling leads to time-consuming and expensive repairs.
notes.example: Like the spark you feel from a door handle, but silent: touching the mating pins of a circuit card can be enough to damage it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electrostatic Discharge (ESD) Considerations”, PDF p. 446
notes.evidence: One of the most frequent causes of damage to a solidstate component or integrated circuits is the electrostatic discharge (ESD) from the human body when one of these devices is handled.

notes.front: What is magnetism?
notes.back: The property of an object to attract certain metallic substances, generally ferrous materials such as iron and its alloys.
notes.explanation: Its ultimate nature is not fully known, so it is best described by the effects it produces.
notes.example: Like a bar magnet lifting soft iron, but not a copper wire: copper is nonmagnetic.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Magnetism”, PDF p. 447
notes.evidence: Magnetism is defined as the property of an object to attract certain metallic substances.

notes.front: What is electromagnetism?
notes.back: The link between electricity and magnetism: electrons moving through a conductor create a magnetic field around it.
notes.explanation: Oersted showed the field did not come from the conductor’s material, since the copper wire was nonmagnetic; the moving electrons made it.
notes.example: Like a compass needle swinging when held near a wire carrying current, and swinging back when the current stops.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electromagnetism”, PDF p. 453
notes.evidence: The electrons moving through the wire created the magnetic field around the conductor.

notes.front: What is voltage, also called electromotive force (EMF)?
notes.back: The push or pressure, measured between two points, that moves electrons through a conductor; its symbol is E and its unit the volt.
notes.explanation: Unlike current, voltage is not a flow: it is always a value across two points.
notes.example: Like the difference in water pressure between two connected tanks, but electrical: across an aircraft battery’s terminals there are 12 or 24 volts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electromotive Force (Voltage)”, PDF p. 455

notes.front: What is electric current?
notes.back: Electrons in motion: the rate at which charge flows through a conductor, measured in amperes (symbol I).
notes.explanation: It is called current or current flow no matter how many electrons are moving.
notes.example: Like water flowing in a pipe, but made of free electrons drifting through a copper wire towards the positive terminal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Current”, PDF p. 457
notes.evidence: Electrons in motion make up an electric current.

notes.front: What is resistance in a circuit?
notes.back: The property of a conductor that determines how much current flows for a given voltage; it is measured in ohms (Ω), symbol R.
notes.explanation: Resistance is the third property that links the two fundamental properties, current and voltage.
notes.example: Like a narrow section in a water pipe: for the same pressure, a higher resistance lets less current through.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Ohm’s Law (Resistance)”, PDF p. 458
notes.evidence: The resistance of the conductor determines the amount of current that flows under the given voltage.

notes.front: What does Ohm’s law say?
notes.back: Current, voltage and resistance are linearly related: I = E/R, so in most cases more resistance means less current.
notes.explanation: Because the relation is linear, doubling the voltage across a fixed resistor doubles the current through it.
notes.example: Like water pressure in a pipe: double the pressure (voltage) through the same pipe (resistance) and twice as much water (current) flows.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Ohm’s Law (Resistance)”, PDF p. 458
notes.evidence: In most cases, the greater the circuit resistance, the less the current. If the resistance is reduced, then the current increases. This relation is linear in nature and is known as Ohm’s Law.

notes.front: What is Watt’s law, the general power formula?
notes.back: P = I × E: power in watts equals current in amperes times voltage in volts.
notes.explanation: Multiplying voltage (energy per charge) by current (charge per time) cancels the charge and leaves energy per time, which is power.
notes.example: Like working out a heater’s output from its supply: 2 amperes at 12 volts is 24 watts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Power Formulas Used in the Study of Electricity”, PDF p. 463
notes.evidence: can then be given by the equation: General Power Formula P = I (E) Where P = Power I = Current E = Volts

notes.front: What is electrical energy, and how is it found from power?
notes.back: The ability to do work; it is power multiplied by time, in joules, watt-seconds or kilowatt-hours.
notes.explanation: Power is the rate of using energy, so power used over a span of time is energy consumed.
notes.example: Like the reading on a household electricity bill, which counts kilowatt-hours rather than watts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Energy in an Electrical Circuit”, PDF p. 463
notes.evidence: Because power is the rate of energy usage, power used over a span of time is actually energy consumption. If power and time are multiplied together, we get energy.

notes.front: What is a thermistor?
notes.back: A temperature-sensitive variable resistor with a negative temperature coefficient: its resistance falls as temperature rises.
notes.explanation: Negative temperature coefficient means resistance moves the opposite way to the sensed temperature.
notes.example: Like an ordinary resistor, but one whose value drops as the part it senses warms up.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Thermistors”, PDF p. 468
notes.evidence: This component has a negative temperature coefficient, which means that as the sensed temperature increases, the resistance of the thermistor decreases.

notes.front: What is a fuse?
notes.back: A protective device, carrying all the circuit’s current, whose metal strip melts and opens the circuit when current exceeds its rating.
notes.explanation: Because it opens by melting, a fuse protects the circuit from over-current but must then be replaced.
notes.example: Like a weak link in a chain: a 5-amp fuse passes currents up to 5 amps and melts open above that.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Fuse”, PDF p. 469
notes.evidence: The fuse is installed in the circuit so that all the current in the circuit passes through it.

notes.front: What is a current limiter?
notes.back: A fuse-like device with a copper link that withstands a considerable short overload, used in heavy-current circuits of 30 amps or more.
notes.explanation: It is used mainly to sectionalise an aircraft circuit or bus, and like a fuse it must be replaced once open.
notes.example: Like a fuse, but built for heavy circuits such as a main bus, and shown on schematics as two triangles pointing at each other.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Current Limiter”, PDF p. 470
notes.evidence: The current limiter is very much like the fuse. However, the current limiter link is usually made of copper and will stand a considerable overload for a short period of time.

notes.front: What is a circuit breaker?
notes.back: A device, often used in place of a fuse, that breaks the circuit when current exceeds a set value and can then be reset.
notes.explanation: Being resettable is what sets it apart from a fuse or current limiter, which must be replaced.
notes.example: Like a fuse that can be pushed back in after it trips, grouped with others on a panel the flight crew can reach.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Circuit Breaker”, PDF p. 470
notes.evidence: The circuit breaker is commonly used in place of a fuse and is designed to break the circuit and stop the current flow when the current exceeds a predetermined value.

notes.front: What is an arc fault circuit breaker?
notes.back: A breaker that monitors the circuit for an electrical arcing signature, which can indicate wiring faults and unsafe conditions.
notes.explanation: It adds a layer of protection beyond the thermal protection of conventional breakers, since arcing can lead to fires or loss of power to critical systems.
notes.example: Like a conventional breaker with a listener added: it reacts to the signature of arcing, not only to overheating.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Arc Fault Circuit Breaker”, PDF p. 470
notes.evidence: The arc fault circuit breaker monitors the circuit for an electrical arcing signature, which can indicate possible wiring faults and unsafe conditions.

notes.front: What is a thermal protector?
notes.back: A switch that protects a motor by opening the circuit automatically when the motor’s temperature becomes excessively high.
notes.explanation: It has just two positions, open and closed, and its most common use is to keep a motor from overheating.
notes.example: Like a circuit breaker, but tripped by the motor’s heat rather than by the current in the wires.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Thermal Protectors”, PDF p. 470
notes.evidence: A thermal protector, or switch, is used to protect a motor. It is designed to open the circuit automatically whenever the temperature of the motor becomes excessively high.

notes.front: What is a relay?
notes.back: An electromechanical switch in which a small current, through its coil, controls a large current.
notes.explanation: Energising the coil makes an electromagnet that pulls the relay’s arm across to the other set of contacts.
notes.example: Like a toggle switch, but thrown by an electromagnet: a small flight deck switch can energise a coil that closes a heavy-current circuit.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Relays”, PDF p. 474
notes.evidence: A relay is simply an electromechanical switch where a small amount of current can control a large amount of current.

notes.front: What does Kirchhoff’s voltage law state?
notes.back: The algebraic sum of all voltages around a closed loop is zero: the voltage drops add up to the source voltage.
notes.explanation: The source’s sign is opposite to the drops’ signs, so around the loop they cancel.
notes.example: Like money in a budget: a 24-volt source spent as drops of 14 volts and 10 volts leaves nothing over.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law”, PDF p. 477
notes.evidence: This law simply states that the algebraic sum of all voltages around a closed path or loop is zero. Another way of saying it: the sum of all the voltage drops equals the total source voltage.

notes.front: What does Kirchhoff’s current law state?
notes.back: The sum of the currents flowing into a junction (node) equals the sum of the currents flowing out of it.
notes.explanation: A junction is where two or more circuit paths meet, such as where parallel branches join.
notes.example: Like water at a pipe tee: 10 litres a minute in means 10 litres a minute out, however it divides between the branches.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Kirchhoff’s Current Law”, PDF p. 482
notes.evidence: Kirchhoff’s Current Law can be stated as: the sum of the currents into a junction or node is equal to the sum of the currents flowing out of that same junction or node.

notes.front: What does Faraday’s law (the law of electromagnetic induction) say?
notes.back: Moving a magnetic field relative to a coil induces a voltage across it, proportional to the rate of change of the field.
notes.explanation: If the coil forms a complete circuit, a current is induced as well as a voltage.
notes.example: Like pushing a bar magnet into a coil wired to a meter: the needle moves while the magnet moves, and reads zero when it stops.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Characteristics of Inductance”, PDF p. 497
notes.evidence: Michael Faraday discovered that by moving a magnet through a coil of wire, a voltage was induced across the coil. If a complete circuit was provided, then a current was also induced. The amount of induced voltage is directly proportional to the rate of change of the magnetic field with respect to the coil.

notes.front: What does Lenz’s law state?
notes.back: A current induced by relative motion of a conductor and a magnetic field flows so that its own magnetic field opposes the motion.
notes.explanation: The induced current always works against the change that produced it.
notes.example: Like a magnet pushed into a coil meeting a push back: the coil’s induced field opposes the magnet coming in.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Generator Principles”, PDF p. 485
notes.evidence: Lenz’s Law states that the induced current caused by the relative motion of a conductor and a magnetic field always flows in such a direction that its magnetic field opposes the motion.

notes.front: What is frequency in an alternating current circuit?
notes.back: The number of complete cycles of alternating current per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
notes.explanation: A cycle is one full series of changes, positive and negative alternation, before the pattern repeats.
notes.example: Like counting laps per minute on a track: 400 complete cycles each second is 400 hertz.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Cycle and Frequency”, PDF p. 488
notes.evidence: second). The standard unit of frequency measurement is the hertz (Hz).

notes.front: What is capacitance?
notes.back: The measure of a capacitor’s ability to store charge; its symbol is C and its unit the farad.
notes.explanation: A capacitor is two parallel plates separated by a nonconductor, the dielectric, acting as a reservoir for electricity.
notes.example: Like a small tank that fills with charge: a capacitor charged from a battery keeps its charge when the switch is opened.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Capacitance”, PDF p. 491
notes.evidence: The measure of a capacitor’s ability to store charge is its capacitance. The symbol used for capacitance is the letter C.

notes.front: What is capacitive reactance XC?
notes.back: A capacitor’s opposition to alternating current, measured in ohms: XC = 1 ÷ (2πfC).
notes.explanation: It falls as frequency or capacitance rises, because the capacitor then never builds up a full opposing charge.
notes.example: Like resistance, but it depends on frequency: the same capacitor opposes a low frequency far more than a high one.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Capacitive Reactance Xc”, PDF p. 496
notes.evidence: The actual AC reactance Xc, which just like resistance, is measured in ohms (Ω).

notes.front: What is inductance?
notes.back: The property of a coil to oppose any change in the current through it; its symbol is L and its unit the henry (H).
notes.explanation: A changing current makes a changing field, which induces an emf in the coil that opposes the change.
notes.example: Like a flywheel in a current path: it resists the current starting and resists it stopping.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Characteristics of Inductance”, PDF p. 497
notes.evidence: The primary aspect of the operation of a coil is its property to oppose any change in current through it. This property is called inductance.

notes.front: What is inductive reactance XL?
notes.back: The opposition an inductance gives to alternating current, measured in ohms: XL = 2πfL.
notes.explanation: Alternating current changes constantly, so the coil keeps inducing a voltage that opposes the current.
notes.example: Like capacitive reactance, but reversed: raising the frequency raises XL instead of lowering it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Inductive Reactance”, PDF p. 499
notes.evidence: This opposition is called inductive reactance, symbolized by XL, and is measured in ohms just as resistance is measured.

notes.front: What is impedance (Z)?
notes.back: The total opposition to current in an alternating current circuit: resistance, inductive reactance and capacitive reactance combined, in ohms.
notes.explanation: With resistance only, impedance equals resistance and Ohm’s law becomes I = E/Z.
notes.example: Like resistance for a lamp or heater, but for a motor coil it also includes the coil’s reactance.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Ohm’s Law for AC Circuits”, PDF p. 500
notes.evidence: The combined effects of resistance, inductive reactance, and capacitive reactance make up the total opposition to current flow in an AC circuit. This total opposition is called impedance and is represented by the letter Z.

notes.front: What is resonance in AC circuits?
notes.back: The condition at the resonant frequency, where inductive and capacitive reactance are equal and cancel, leaving only resistance.
notes.explanation: Lowering frequency lowers inductive reactance but raises capacitive reactance, so at one frequency they meet.
notes.example: Like two equal tug-of-war teams: the reactances pull opposite ways and cancel, so only the resistance limits the current.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Resonance”, PDF p. 504
notes.evidence: At some particular frequency, known as the resonant frequency, the reactive effects of a capacitor and an inductor is equal.

notes.front: What is a transformer?
notes.back: A device that changes electrical energy at one voltage into electrical energy at a different voltage.
notes.explanation: It works by mutual induction: a varying field from the primary winding induces a voltage in the secondary.
notes.example: Like a gearbox for voltage: a step-down transformer with five times as many primary turns as secondary turns gives one-fifth of the voltage.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Transformers”, PDF p. 506
notes.evidence: A transformer changes electrical energy of a given voltage into electrical energy at a different voltage level.

notes.front: What is a current transformer used for?
notes.back: To sense alternating current generator line current and supply a proportional current to protection and control devices.
notes.explanation: It is a ring-type transformer that uses a current-carrying power lead as its primary.
notes.example: Like a clamp round a generator power lead: the lead itself is the primary, and the ring gives a small matching current.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Current Transformers”, PDF p. 508
notes.evidence: Current transformers are used in AC power supply systems to sense generator line current and to provide a current, proportional to the line current, for circuit protection and control devices.

notes.front: What is the D’Arsonval meter movement?
notes.back: A basic direct current meter movement, used in ammeters, voltmeters and ohmmeters, whose pointer deflects in proportion to the current through its coil.
notes.explanation: It is fundamentally a current-measuring device; the meters differ in how they are connected.
notes.example: Like the needle movement at the heart of an analogue multimeter, which reads zero if connected to alternating current.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “D’Arsonval Meter Movement”, PDF p. 509
notes.evidence: This basic DC type of meter movement—first employed by the French scientist, d’Arsonval, in making electrical measurement—is a current measuring device, which is used in the ammeter, voltmeter, and ohmmeter.

notes.front: What is a megohmmeter (megger)?
notes.back: A high-range ohmmeter with a hand-operated generator, used to measure insulation resistance and other high resistances.
notes.explanation: Its chief advantage over an ohmmeter is measuring at a high potential, or breakdown voltage.
notes.example: Like an ohmmeter, but cranked by hand to test whether wiring insulation will leak under electrical stress.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Megger (Megohmmeter)”, PDF p. 513
notes.evidence: The megger, or megohmmeter, is a high range ohmmeter containing a hand-operated generator. It is used to measure insulation resistance and other high-resistance values.

notes.front: What does an oscilloscope let a technician do?
notes.back: See and quantify waveform characteristics such as phase relationships, amplitudes and durations.
notes.explanation: Bench oscilloscopes traditionally display the waveform on a cathode-ray tube.
notes.example: Like a voltmeter that draws a picture: instead of one number, it shows the whole sine wave over time.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Frequency Measurement/Oscilloscope”, PDF p. 517
notes.evidence: The viewing capabilities of the oscilloscope make it possible to see and quantify various waveform characteristics, such as phase relationships, amplitudes, and durations.

notes.front: What is a digital multimeter (DMM), and why has it become more common than analogue meters?
notes.back: A digital meter combining voltmeter, ammeter and ohmmeter functions; it is easier to read and more accurate.
notes.explanation: An analogue multimeter’s single-coil movement needs several scales that are not always easy to read accurately.
notes.example: Like the older volt-ohm-milliammeter, but with a numeric display instead of a needle and scales.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Digital Multimeter”, PDF p. 519
notes.evidence: Digital multimeters (DMM) and digital voltmeters (DVM) are more common due to their ease of use. These meters are easier to read and provide greater accuracy when compared to the older analog units with needle movement.

notes.front: What is the most common battery rating, and how is it found?
notes.back: The ampere-hour rating of capacity: current in amperes multiplied by the hours of discharge.
notes.explanation: For aircraft batteries, capacity is rated over a 5-hour discharge, which is a basis for rating, not an expected service time.
notes.example: Like a fuel tank size: a 1 ampere-hour battery should supply 1 amp for an hour, or 2 amps for half an hour.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Battery Ratings”, PDF p. 530
notes.evidence: The most common battery rating is the ampere-hour rating. This is a unit of measurement for battery capacity. It is determined by multiplying a current flow in amperes by the time in hours that the battery is being discharged.

notes.front: What is a nickel-cadmium (NiCad) battery?
notes.back: A secondary battery with nickel hydroxide positive plates, cadmium negative plates and potassium hydroxide electrolyte; about 1.25 volts per cell.
notes.explanation: It is usually interchangeable with the lead-acid type, but its alkaline electrolyte needs different handling.
notes.example: Like a lead-acid aircraft battery in use, but alkaline inside: its electrolyte is caustic rather than acid.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Nickel-Cadmium Batteries”, PDF p. 533
notes.evidence: The typical open circuit cell voltage of a nickel-cadmium battery is about 1.25 volts.

notes.front: What is a sealed lead acid (SLA) battery, and why is it gaining use?
notes.back: A sealed lead-acid battery increasingly used instead of flooded lead-acid and NiCad batteries, notably for standby and emergency packs.
notes.explanation: It has no voltage depression, so it needs no scheduled deep-cycle maintenance or special test equipment.
notes.example: Like a NiCad emergency pack for a standby attitude gyro, but with cell matching built in and no memory effect.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Sealed Lead Acid (SLA) Batteries”, PDF p. 533
notes.evidence: In many applications, sealed lead acid (SLA) batteries are gaining in use over flooded lead acid and Ni-Cad batteries.

notes.front: What is a lithium-ion battery, and what special hazard does it carry?
notes.back: A rechargeable battery now certified for aircraft; unlike other rechargeables it has a flammable electrolyte and is kept pressurised.
notes.explanation: Under certain conditions these batteries can overheat and a fire can occur.
notes.example: Like the battery in a mobile phone or laptop, but scaled up: the Boeing 787 uses two large 32-volt, 8-cell units.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Lithium-Ion Batteries”, PDF p. 534
notes.evidence: Lithium-ion batteries can be dangerous under some conditions and can pose a safety hazard since they contain, unlike other rechargeable batteries, a flammable electrolyte and are also kept pressurized.

notes.front: What does an inverter do in an aircraft electrical system?
notes.back: It converts part of the aircraft’s direct current power to alternating current, mainly for instruments, radio, radar and lighting.
notes.explanation: Aircraft inverters usually supply 400-cycle current, and come in two basic types: rotary and static.
notes.example: Like a travel adaptor run backwards: a direct current battery feeds it, and 115-volt or 26-volt alternating current comes out.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Inverters”, PDF p. 534
notes.evidence: An inverter is used in some aircraft systems to convert a portion of the aircraft’s DC power to AC. This AC is used mainly for instruments, radio, radar, lighting, and other accessories.

notes.front: What is a rectifier?
notes.back: A device that transforms alternating current into direct current by limiting the direction of current flow.
notes.explanation: Solid-state (semiconductor) rectifiers have replaced virtually all other types.
notes.example: Like a one-way valve in a water line: current may pass one way and is blocked the other.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Rectifiers”, PDF p. 541
notes.evidence: A rectifier is a device that transforms AC into DC by limiting or regulating the direction of current flow.

notes.front: What is a Zener diode?
notes.back: A breakdown diode designed to conduct in reverse once the voltage reaches its set reverse bias voltage, then acting as a constant voltage source.
notes.explanation: Below that voltage it blocks like any reverse-biased diode, which lets it work as a voltage regulator.
notes.example: Like a pressure relief valve: it stays shut below its set voltage and opens to hold the voltage steady above it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Zener Diodes”, PDF p. 544
notes.evidence: Once a specific reverse bias voltage has been reached, the diode conducts and behaves like a constant voltage source.

notes.front: What is a light-emitting diode (LED)?
notes.back: A forward-biased diode that gives off the energy of electrons falling into holes as light rather than heat.
notes.explanation: In a rectifier diode the same energy is lost as heat.
notes.example: Like a flight deck indicator lamp, but without a filament: it lasts longer, runs cooler and switches faster.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Light-Emitting Diode (LED)”, PDF p. 544
notes.evidence: In a rectifier diode, this energy is dissipated as heat. However, in the light-emitting diode (LED), the energy is dissipated as light.

notes.front: What is a transistor?
notes.back: A three-terminal device used mainly to amplify signals and control current; it is classed NPN or PNP.
notes.explanation: The class depends on how its N-type and P-type materials are arranged.
notes.example: Like a tap worked by a small hand: a small base signal controls a larger current through the device.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Introduction to Transistors”, PDF p. 546
notes.evidence: The transistor is a three-terminal device primarily used to amplify signals and control current within a circuit.

notes.front: How does a field effect transistor (FET) differ from a bipolar transistor?
notes.back: It has only one junction of P-type and N-type material and is voltage-controlled; the bipolar transistor is current-controlled.
notes.explanation: Its reverse-biased gate looks like a very high resistance to the circuit, so it has little insertion influence.
notes.example: Like a bipolar transistor, but steered by voltage on its gate rather than by base current.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Field Effect Transistors”, PDF p. 549
notes.evidence: is a current-controlled device, while the FET has only one PN junction and is a voltage-controlled device.

notes.front: What is an operational amplifier (OP AMP)?
notes.back: A usually high-gain amplifier, used with other components for computing functions or filtering; its gain is set by feedback.
notes.explanation: Originally made for analogue computers, it is now used in amplifiers, comparators, oscillators and filters.
notes.example: Like a general-purpose building block on a chip: the same small device becomes a comparator or a filter depending on the parts around it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Operational Amplifiers (OP AMP)”, PDF p. 557
notes.evidence: An operational amplifier (OP AMP) is designed to be used with other circuit components and performs either computing functions or filtering.

notes.front: What is an integrated circuit (IC), and what are its advantages over discrete components?
notes.back: A single package holding logic functions and other components; it is smaller, uses less power, is very reliable and inexpensive.
notes.explanation: Its most noticeable feature is size: it can be thousands of times smaller than discrete parts.
notes.example: Like a whole circuit board of gates shrunk onto one chip.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “The Integrated Circuit”, PDF p. 563
notes.evidence: In most cases, the IC has an advantage over the use of discrete components in that they are smaller, consume less power, are very reliable, and are inexpensive.

notes.front: Why do digital computers use binary numbers?
notes.back: Because the only two truth values, true and false, can be represented by the binary digits 1 and 0.
notes.explanation: A circuit in computer memory can be open or closed according to the value assigned to it.
notes.example: Like a row of switches, each either on (1) or off (0).
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Logic Circuits”, PDF p. 562
notes.evidence: It is employed in the binary system used by digital computers primarily because the only truth values (true and false) can be represented by the binary digits 1 and 0.

notes.front: What is a DC generator, and what are its major parts?
notes.back: A generator whose commutator delivers direct current; its major parts are a field frame (yoke), a rotating armature and a brush assembly.
notes.explanation: The loop generates alternating voltage just as in an alternator; the commutator’s switching makes it direct.
notes.example: Like a simple alternating current generator, but with the slip rings replaced by a split commutator.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Construction Features of DC Generators”, PDF p. 569
notes.evidence: The major parts, or assemblies, of a DC generator are a field frame (or yoke), a rotating armature, and a brush assembly.

notes.front: What is armature reaction?
notes.back: Distortion of a generator’s main magnetic field by the fields that armature current sets up; it grows with load.
notes.explanation: The distortion causes sparking at the brushes, pitting the commutator, wearing the brushes and reducing output.
notes.example: Like a crosswind pushing a flag off line: the armature’s own field pushes the main field, shifting the neutral plane.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Armature Reaction”, PDF p. 572
notes.evidence: Since armature current increases with load, the distortion becomes greater with an increase in load. This distortion of the magnetic field is called armature reaction.

notes.front: What principle makes a DC motor turn?
notes.back: A current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field has a force produced on it that makes it rotate.
notes.explanation: The commutator switches the coil’s connections between the brushes twice per revolution.
notes.example: Like a DC generator run backwards: current is fed in and rotation comes out.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Developing Torque”, PDF p. 579
notes.evidence: Developing Torque If a coil in which current is flowing is placed in a magnetic field, a force is produced which causes the coil to rotate.

notes.front: What is counter electromotive force (CEMF) in a motor?
notes.back: The voltage generated in a motor’s rotating armature, opposite to the applied voltage; it rises with speed and limits armature current.
notes.explanation: That is why a running 28-volt motor draws a few amperes, not the hundreds its low armature resistance alone would allow.
notes.example: Like a generator hidden inside every motor, pushing back against the supply as the armature speeds up.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Counter Electromotive Force (emf)”, PDF p. 583
notes.evidence: This voltage is called the back or counter emf and is opposite in direction to the voltage applied to the motor from the external source.

notes.front: What is an induction motor, and what is its slip?
notes.back: An alternating current motor (squirrel cage) whose rotor is turned by a rotating stator field; slip is how far the rotor lags that field’s speed.
notes.explanation: The rotor must turn slightly slower than the field so that current is still induced in it.
notes.example: Like a dog on a lead trotting just behind its owner: the rotor follows the rotating field a little slower.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Three-Phase Induction Motor”, PDF p. 590
notes.evidence: This difference in speed is called slip and is expressed as a percentage of the synchronous speed.

notes.front: What is a synchronous motor?
notes.back: An alternating current motor whose rotor is dragged round at exactly the speed of the stator’s rotating magnetic field.
notes.explanation: Unlike the induction motor, its torque does not depend on currents induced in the rotor; the rotor has its own field.
notes.example: Like an electric clock motor, locked in step with the supply frequency.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Synchronous Motor”, PDF p. 592
notes.evidence: The synchronous motor is so designed and constructed that these two fields react to each other in such a manner that the rotor is dragged along and rotates at the same speed as the rotating magnetic field produced by the stator windings.

notes.front: What is an alternator?
notes.back: A generator that produces alternating current, converting mechanical energy into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction.
notes.explanation: The Handbook uses “alternator” to distinguish alternating current generators from direct current ones.
notes.example: Like a DC generator, but with slip rings instead of a commutator, so its output stays alternating.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Basic Alternators & Classifications”, PDF p. 595
notes.evidence: An electrical generator is a machine that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction.

notes.front: What is regulated to control a generator’s voltage output, and why that factor?
notes.back: The field current: of the factors that set output voltage, it is the only one that can be conveniently controlled.
notes.explanation: Efficient operation of the aircraft’s equipment depends on a constant voltage supply from the generator.
notes.example: Like a dimmer on the field winding: more field resistance, less field current, a weaker field and lower output.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Regulation of Generator Voltage”, PDF p. 600
notes.evidence: Among the factors, which determine the voltage output of a generator, only one, the strength of the field current, can be conveniently controlled.

notes.front: What is a generator control unit (GCU)?
notes.back: A unit, most often on turbine aircraft, that performs regulation, sensing and protection functions for the generating system.
notes.explanation: Its most basic function is voltage regulation: comparing the sensed output with a reference voltage.
notes.example: Like a voltage regulator with a protection panel attached: it also handles overvoltage, paralleling and reverse current.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Basic Functions of a Generator Control Unit (GCU)”, PDF p. 605
notes.evidence: The generator control unit (GCU) is more commonly found on turbine power aircraft. The most basic GCU perform a number of functions related to the regulation, sensing, and protection of the DC generation system.

notes.front: What is a constant speed drive (CSD), and why is it needed?
notes.back: A hydraulic transmission between engine and alternator that keeps the alternator speed, and so its frequency, constant as engine speed varies.
notes.explanation: Alternating current equipment is designed for a set voltage and frequency, but engine speed varies.
notes.example: Like an automatic gearbox for the alternator: the engine speeds up and slows down, the alternator keeps turning at one speed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Alternator Constant Speed Drive System”, PDF p. 605
notes.evidence: Since the various electrical devices operating on AC supplied by alternators are designed to operate at a certain voltage and at a specified frequency, the speed of the alternators must be constant; however, the speed of an airplane engine varies.

notes.front: At the centre of the atom is the {{c1::nucleus}}, which contains the protons and neutrons.
notes.explanation: Protons carry a positive charge and neutrons are neutral, so the nucleus as a whole is positive.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electrons, Protons, & Neutrons”, PDF p. 442
notes.evidence: At the center of the atom is the nucleus, which contains protons and neutrons. Protons are positively-charged particles, and neutrons are neutrally-charged particles.

notes.front: An atom has a neutral charge when the total positive charge of its protons {{c1::equals}} the total negative charge of its electrons.
notes.explanation: The two kinds of charge cancel only when they balance exactly.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electrons, Protons, & Neutrons”, PDF p. 443
notes.evidence: When the total positive charge of the protons in the nucleus equals the total negative charge of the electrons in orbit around the nucleus, the atom is said to have a neutral charge.

notes.front: A neutral atom gains two extra electrons from a neighbouring material. What has it become?
notes.back: D) A negative ion (anion)
notes.choices:
A) A positive ion (cation)
B) A neutral atom with a larger nucleus
C) A free electron
D) A negative ion (anion)
notes.choicesExplained: A) A cation is an atom that has lost electrons, not gained them. B) Electrons orbit the nucleus; gaining them does not change the nucleus or leave the atom neutral. C) A free electron is a single dislodged electron, not an atom.
notes.explanation: Extra electrons give the atom more negative than positive charge, which is what a negative ion is.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Ions”, PDF p. 443
notes.evidence: An atom that has gained an extra number of electrons is negatively charged and is called a negative ion or an anion.

notes.front: What does the valence of an atom determine?
notes.back: Its ability to gain or lose an electron, and so its chemical and electrical properties.
notes.explanation: Those properties decide whether the material behaves as a conductor, semiconductor or insulator.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Conductors, Insulators, and Semiconductors”, PDF p. 443
notes.evidence: The valence of an atom determines its ability to gain or lose an electron, which ultimately determines the chemical and electrical properties of the atom.

notes.front: What happens to a free electron once it is dislodged from its atom?
notes.back: It can travel from atom to atom, becoming the flow of electrons called current.
notes.explanation: This drift of freed electrons is what a practical electrical circuit uses as current.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Free Electrons”, PDF p. 443
notes.evidence: Once freed from the atom, the electron can then travel from atom to atom, becoming the flow of electrons commonly called current in a practical electrical circuit.

notes.front: Which three elements does the Handbook name as good conductors because they have many free electrons?
notes.back: Gold, copper and silver.
notes.explanation: Their atoms have a few loosely bound outer electrons, which heat can break loose to drift through the material.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Conductors”, PDF p. 444
notes.evidence: Elements such as gold, copper, and silver possess many free electrons and make good conductors.

notes.front: What is breakdown in an insulator?
notes.back: Its outer electrons being dislodged by an extremely strong electrical field; it usually damages the insulator physically.
notes.explanation: Under normal conditions an insulator produces no free electrons, so only a very strong field can force them out.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Insulators”, PDF p. 445
notes.evidence: Only when the material is in an extremely strong electrical field will the outer electrons be dislodged. This action is called breakdown and usually causes physical damage to the insulator.

notes.front: How do conductors and insulators differ in their free electrons?
notes.back: Conductors have many free electrons; insulators normally produce none, so current cannot be conducted through them.
notes.explanation: Current is the flow of free electrons, so a material without them has nothing to carry it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Insulators”, PDF p. 445
notes.evidence: Under normal conditions, atoms in these materials do not produce free electrons. The absence of free electrons means that electrical current cannot be conducted through the material.

notes.front: Glass, ceramic and plastic: conductors, insulators or semiconductors?
notes.back: Insulators.
notes.explanation: They conduct current very poorly or not at all.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Insulators”, PDF p. 444
notes.evidence: Insulators are materials that do not conduct electrical current very well or not at all, such as glass, ceramic, and plastic.

notes.front: Which two materials are the most widely used semiconductors?
notes.back: Silicon and germanium.
notes.explanation: Semiconductors are the materials transistors and integrated circuits are made from.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Semiconductors”, PDF p. 445
notes.evidence: Semiconductors are used to make transistors and integrated circuits. Silicon and germanium are the most widely used semiconductor materials.

notes.front: What does the prefix kilo (k) mean?
notes.back: One thousand (1,000).
notes.explanation: Kilo is one of the most used conversion factors: a kilovolt is 1,000 volts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Metric Based Prefixes Used for Electrical Calculations”, PDF p. 445
notes.evidence: Kilo (k) means one thousand (1,000).

notes.front: What does the prefix micro (μ) mean?
notes.back: One-millionth (1/1,000,000).
notes.explanation: It is one of the four prefixes most commonly used in electrical work.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Metric Based Prefixes Used for Electrical Calculations”, PDF p. 445
notes.evidence: Micro (μ) means one-millionth (1⁄1,000,000).

notes.front: A test set is labelled 2.5 kV. How many volts is that?
notes.back: B) 2,500 volts
notes.choices:
A) 25 volts
B) 2,500 volts
C) 0.0025 volts
D) 2,500,000 volts
notes.choicesExplained: A) That would need a factor of 10, which is not kilo. C) That treats kilo as one-thousandth, which is milli. D) That treats kilo as mega (one million).
notes.explanation: Kilo means 1,000, so 2.5 kV is 2.5 × 1,000 volts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Metric Based Prefixes Used for Electrical Calculations”, PDF p. 445
notes.evidence: Kilo means 1,000, and when used with volts, is expressed as kilovolt, meaning 1,000 volts.

notes.front: What usually causes static electricity?
notes.back: Non-conductive materials, such as rubber, plastic or glass, rubbed together so that electrons transfer and the charges become unbalanced.
notes.explanation: The unbalanced charges are why the two objects then attract or repel each other.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Static Electricity”, PDF p. 445
notes.evidence: Static electricity is usually caused when non-conductive materials, such as rubber, plastic, or glass, are rubbed together causing a transfer of electrons, which results in an imbalance of charges between the two materials.

notes.front: What is the difference between static and dynamic electricity?
notes.back: Whether the electrons are at rest (static) or in motion (dynamic).
notes.explanation: The Handbook bases the distinction simply on electron movement, not on the amount of charge.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Static Electricity”, PDF p. 445
notes.evidence: The difference between the two is based simply on whether the electrons are at rest (static) or in motion (dynamic).

notes.front: Like charges {{c1::repel}} each other and unlike charges attract each other.
notes.explanation: This is one of the most fundamental laws of static electricity, and magnetism follows the same pattern.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Attractive and Repulsive Forces”, PDF p. 445
notes.evidence: Like charges repel each other and unlike charges attract each other.

notes.front: Two suspended light balls have both been given a surplus of electrons. What happens when they hang close together?
notes.back: D) They repel each other
notes.choices:
A) They attract each other
B) They neither attract nor repel
C) They exchange protons until neutral
D) They repel each other
notes.choicesExplained: A) Attraction happens between unlike charges, and both balls are negative. B) Charged objects always exert a force on each other. C) Protons stay in the nucleus; it is electrons that transfer.
notes.explanation: Both balls carry negative charge, and like charges repel.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Attractive and Repulsive Forces”, PDF p. 445
notes.evidence: All electrons possess a negative charge and as such repel each other.

notes.front: What three ways does the Handbook give to avoid ESD damage when handling a removed unit?
notes.back: Touch the removed box’s chassis to discharge your body, wear a grounding wrist strap, and handle components professionally.
notes.explanation: Each removes or avoids the body’s static charge before it can reach a sensitive component.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electrostatic Discharge (ESD) Considerations”, PDF p. 446
notes.evidence: Damage can be avoided by discharging the static electricity from your body by touching the chassis of the removed box, by wearing a grounding wrist strap, and exercising good professional handling of the components in the aircraft.

notes.front: Ohmmeter ranges that need more than {{c1::one milliampere}} in the test circuit should not be used for testing transistors.
notes.explanation: The Handbook lists this among the precautions for electronic components, alongside keeping test voltages within limits.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electrostatic Discharge (ESD) Considerations”, PDF p. 446
notes.evidence: Ohmmeter ranges that require a current of more than one milliampere in the test circuit should not be used for testing transistors.

notes.front: A technician has just removed an avionics box and is about to pull out one of its circuit cards. What should come first?
notes.back: B) Touch the chassis of the removed box to discharge body static
notes.choices:
A) Rest the card on the carpeted toolbox lid while working
B) Touch the chassis of the removed box to discharge body static
C) Check the card’s mating pins with a finger for damage
D) Pry the card free quickly to limit handling time
notes.choicesExplained: A) A carpet-covered toolbox top is itself an ESD source. C) Touching the mating pins is exactly how ESD damage occurs. D) The Handbook says not to pry components of a circuit board.
notes.explanation: Discharging the body’s static through the chassis first removes the charge that would otherwise reach the card.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electrostatic Discharge (ESD) Considerations”, PDF p. 446
notes.evidence: Damage can be avoided by discharging the static electricity from your body by touching the chassis of the removed box

notes.front: By convention, where do magnetic lines of force leave and enter a magnet?
notes.back: They leave the North pole and enter the South pole.
notes.explanation: The lines form a continuous loop, so no real start point exists; the direction is assumed arbitrarily.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Magnetism”, PDF p. 450
notes.evidence: Arbitrarily, it is assumed that all lines of force leave the North pole of any magnet and enter at the South pole.

notes.front: Is there an insulator for magnetic flux?
notes.back: No: flux passes through all materials, though through some more easily than others.
notes.explanation: Instruments are therefore shielded by giving the flux an easier path around them, not by blocking it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Magnetism”, PDF p. 450
notes.evidence: There is no known insulator for magnetic flux, or lines of force, since they pass through all materials.

notes.front: What is permeability?
notes.back: The measure of the ease with which magnetic flux can penetrate a material; a perfect vacuum is rated one.
notes.explanation: Soft iron and other ferrous metals have high permeability, which is why flux prefers to travel through them.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Magnetism”, PDF p. 450
notes.evidence: Materials such as soft iron and other ferrous metals are said to have a high permeability, the measure of the ease with which magnetic flux can penetrate a material.

notes.front: Why should a magnet not be heated, hammered or dropped?
notes.back: Heat or sudden shock misaligns its molecules, reducing the magnet’s strength.
notes.explanation: A magnet’s strength depends on its molecular magnets staying lined up North to South.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Magnetism”, PDF p. 449
notes.evidence: When handling a magnet, avoid applying direct heat, hammering, or dropping it. Heating or sudden shock creates misalignment of the molecules, causing the strength of a magnet to decrease.

notes.front: A sensitive instrument must be protected from a nearby magnet’s flux. Which approach does the Handbook’s description support?
notes.back: A) Surround it with soft iron, giving the flux an easier path
notes.choices:
A) Surround it with soft iron, giving the flux an easier path
B) Wrap it in rubber, a good electrical insulator
C) Surround it with an air gap of a few centimetres
D) Coat it in a nonmagnetic plastic
notes.choicesExplained: B) There is no known insulator for magnetic flux; rubber does not block it. C) Air has a permeability of about one and offers no easier path. D) Nonmagnetic materials are rated close to one, like air, so they do not divert the flux.
notes.explanation: Flux takes the path of greater permeability, so a soft iron surround guides it away from the instrument.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Magnetism”, PDF p. 450
notes.evidence: Thus, it is possible to shield items, such as instruments, from the effects of the flux by surrounding them with a material that offers an easier path for the lines of force.

notes.front: What distinguishes a permanent magnet from a temporary magnet?
notes.back: A permanent magnet keeps its magnetism long after the magnetising force is removed; a temporary one quickly loses most of it.
notes.explanation: Both are artificial magnets; natural lodestones have no practical use.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Types of Magnets”, PDF p. 450
notes.evidence: Artificial magnets can be further classified as permanent magnets, which retain their magnetism long after the magnetizing force has been removed, and temporary magnets, which quickly lose most of their magnetism when the external magnetizing force is removed.

notes.front: What is residual magnetism, and where does it matter?
notes.back: The small magnetism left in soft iron after the magnetising force is removed; it matters greatly in generator operation.
notes.explanation: Soft iron magnetises easily but loses most of its magnetism quickly, leaving only this small remainder.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Types of Magnets”, PDF p. 452
notes.evidence: The small amount of magnetism remaining, called residual magnetism, is of great importance in such electrical applications as generator operation.

notes.front: What happens to the magnetic field around a conductor when the current stops?
notes.back: It collapses and the magnetism around the conductor disappears.
notes.explanation: The field exists only while current flows; a steady direct current keeps it stationary.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electromagnetism”, PDF p. 453
notes.evidence: When the current stops, the magnetic field collapses and the magnetism around the conductor disappears.

notes.front: What is the left-hand rule for a current-carrying conductor?
notes.back: Grasp the conductor in the left hand with the thumb along the current flow; the fingers wrap in the direction of the magnetic field.
notes.explanation: It finds the direction of the lines of force when the direction of the current is known.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electromagnetism”, PDF p. 453
notes.evidence: If the conductor is grasped in the left hand, with the thumb pointing in the direction of current flow, the fingers will be wrapped around the conductor in the same direction as the lines of the magnetic field. This is called the left-hand rule.

notes.front: What two things does a soft iron core do for a current-carrying coil?
notes.back: It increases the magnetic flux and concentrates the flux lines more highly.
notes.explanation: Soft iron has a greater permeability than air, so the lines of force gather in the core.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electromagnetism”, PDF p. 454
notes.evidence: The addition of the soft iron core does two things for the current carrying coil. First, the magnetic flux is increased. Second, the flux lines are more highly concentrated.

notes.front: How does a solenoid switch work?
notes.back: A spring-loaded iron core sits off centre in a coil; when the coil is energised the core is pulled in and completes a circuit.
notes.explanation: An iron core near a coil is rapidly pulled to the centre, where the field is strongest, when the coil is energised.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electromagnetism”, PDF p. 455
notes.evidence: This principle is used in the solenoid, also called solenoid switch or relay, in which the iron core is spring-loaded off center and moves to complete a circuit when the coil is energized.

notes.front: The leads to an electromagnet powered by direct current are swapped, reversing the current. What happens to its poles?
notes.back: A) North and South swap ends
notes.choices:
A) North and South swap ends
B) The magnet stops working until the core is replaced
C) The field doubles in strength
D) They stay the same, because the core keeps its magnetism
notes.choicesExplained: D) The core takes the coil’s polarity, so it follows the current. B) The magnet still works; only its polarity changes. C) Strength depends on current, turns and core, not on direction.
notes.explanation: The core is magnetised with the coil’s polarity, and that polarity follows the direction of the current.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electromagnetism”, PDF p. 454
notes.evidence: When direct current flows through the coil, the core becomes magnetized with the same polarity (location of North and South poles) as the coil would have without the core. If the current is reversed, the polarity is also reversed.

notes.front: A design calls for an electromagnet with roughly twice the field strength, using the same core. Which change would give it?
notes.back: B) Double the number of loops in the coil
notes.choices:
A) Replace the soft iron core with an air core
B) Double the number of loops in the coil
C) Reverse the direction of current
D) Halve the current
notes.choicesExplained: A) Removing the soft iron lowers the flux, since iron is what increases and concentrates it. C) Reversing the current reverses polarity, not strength. D) Less current gives a weaker field.
notes.explanation: Field strength rises with the number of loops: doubling them about doubles the field.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electromagnetism”, PDF p. 455
notes.evidence: In a similar manner, doubling the number of loops approximately doubles magnetic field strength.

notes.front: In conventional current theory, in which direction does current flow?
notes.back: From positive (+) to negative (−).
notes.explanation: Franklin reasoned that current left a positive source, the one with an abundance of charge, for a negative one.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Conventional Flow”, PDF p. 455
notes.evidence: It then seemed natural to visualize the flow of current as being from the positive (+) to the negative (−).

notes.front: In electron flow theory, in which direction does current flow?
notes.back: Out of the negative (−) source towards the positive (+), which lacks electrons.
notes.explanation: Later discoveries showed this is what actually happens, the opposite of the conventional view.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electron Flow”, PDF p. 455
notes.evidence: Electron flow is what actually happens when an abundance of electrons flow out of the negative (−) source to an area that lacks electrons or the positive (+) source.

notes.front: The Federal Aviation Administration officially defines current flow using {{c1::electron theory}} (negative to positive).
notes.explanation: Both theories are used in industry, but the official definition is the electron one.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electron Flow”, PDF p. 455
notes.evidence: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) officially defines current flow using electron theory (negative to positive).

notes.front: While troubleshooting, a technician finds one manual drawn in conventional flow and another in electron flow. What matters for the analysis?
notes.back: C) Whichever convention is chosen is used consistently
notes.choices:
A) Only electron flow gives correct troubleshooting results
B) The conventional-flow manual must be discarded
C) Whichever convention is chosen is used consistently
D) Current direction must be measured before any analysis
notes.choicesExplained: A) Both methods are used in industry, and either works for troubleshooting. B) Many current publications use both methods. D) The Handbook says the direction makes little to no difference in practice.
notes.explanation: For troubleshooting, the direction chosen makes little to no difference as long as it is used consistently.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electron Flow”, PDF p. 455
notes.evidence: From the practical standpoint of the technician troubleshooting a system, it makes little to no difference which way current is flowing as long as it is used consistently in the analysis.

notes.front: What makes electrons move from one point to another in a circuit?
notes.back: The potential difference between the two points: electrons move from excess to deficiency when a path exists.
notes.explanation: It is the difference that drives the flow, which is why voltage is always stated between two points.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electromotive Force (Voltage)”, PDF p. 457
notes.evidence: The force that causes this movement is the potential difference in electrical energy between the two points.

notes.front: A technician wants to know the voltage available from a battery. Where must the meter be connected?
notes.back: A) Across the two terminal posts
notes.choices:
A) Across the two terminal posts
B) In line with one battery lead
C) To one terminal only
D) To the battery case and the airframe only
notes.choicesExplained: C) Voltage is a value between two points, so one point cannot give a reading. B) Connecting in line is how current, a flow, is measured. D) The emf the battery offers exists between its two terminal posts.
notes.explanation: Voltage is a potential difference determined between two points, here the two terminal posts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Electromotive Force (Voltage)”, PDF p. 457
notes.evidence: That is to say that between the two terminal posts of the battery, there is an emf of 12 or 24 volts available to push current through a circuit.

notes.front: What is current called when it flows in one direction only?
notes.back: Direct current.
notes.explanation: Current that periodically oscillates back and forth is the other form, alternating current.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Current”, PDF p. 458
notes.evidence: When current flow is one direction, it is called direct current (DC).

notes.front: Five coulombs of charge pass a point in a conductor every second. What is the current?
notes.back: D) 5 amperes
notes.choices:
A) 0.2 amperes
B) 5 ohms
C) 5 volts
D) 5 amperes
notes.choicesExplained: A) That divides time by charge instead of charge by time. C) The volt measures potential difference, not charge flow. B) The ohm measures resistance.
notes.explanation: Current is charge divided by time, and one coulomb per second is one ampere.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Current”, PDF p. 458
notes.evidence: One ampere (A) of current is equivalent to 1 coulomb (C) of charge passing through a conductor in 1 second.

notes.front: How much current does 1 ohm of resistance allow when 1 volt is applied?
notes.back: 1 ampere.
notes.explanation: This is the definition that ties the ohm to the volt and the ampere.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Resistance of a Conductor”, PDF p. 459
notes.evidence: Thus, 1 ohm of resistance limits the current flow to 1 ampere in a conductor to which a voltage of 1 volt is applied.

notes.front: What are the three forms of Ohm’s law?
notes.back: I = E/R, E = I × R and R = E/I.
notes.explanation: If any two of the three quantities are known, the third can be found by transposing the equation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Ohm’s Law (Resistance)”, PDF p. 459
notes.evidence: If any two of these circuit quantities are known, the third may be found by simple algebraic transposition.

notes.front: A 28-volt bus supplies a heater element of 7 ohms. What current does it draw?
notes.back: D) 4 amperes
notes.choices:
A) 196 amperes
B) 0.25 amperes
C) 21 amperes
D) 4 amperes
notes.choicesExplained: A) That multiplies E by R, which gives no quantity in Ohm’s law. B) That divides R by E. C) That subtracts R from E.
notes.explanation: I = E/R, so 28 volts divided by 7 ohms gives 4 amperes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Ohm’s Law (Resistance)”, PDF p. 459
notes.evidence: With this equation, we can calculate current in a circuit if the voltage and resistance are known.

notes.front: A current of 0.5 amperes flows through a 48-ohm lamp. What is the voltage across it?
notes.back: A) 24 volts
notes.choices:
A) 24 volts
B) 96 volts
C) 48.5 volts
D) 0.01 volts
notes.choicesExplained: B) That divides R by I instead of multiplying. C) That adds the two values. D) That divides I by R.
notes.explanation: E = I × R, so 0.5 amperes times 48 ohms is 24 volts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Ohm’s Law (Resistance)”, PDF p. 459
notes.evidence: By multiplying both sides of the equation 1 by R, we get an equivalent form of Ohm’s Law, which is: Equation 2 E = I (R)

notes.front: Copper conducts better than aluminium, so why is aluminium wire often used?
notes.back: It is much lighter, and cheaper, so it is used where weight matters.
notes.explanation: A copper wire has lower resistance than an aluminium wire of the same diameter, but weight and cost can outweigh that.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Factors Affecting Resistance”, PDF p. 459
notes.evidence: However, aluminum is much lighter than copper, and for this reason, as well as cost considerations, aluminum is often used when the weight factor is important.

notes.front: The resistance of a metallic conductor is {{c1::directly}} proportional to its length.
notes.explanation: The longer a wire of a given size, the more resistance the moving electrons meet.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Factors Affecting Resistance”, PDF p. 459
notes.evidence: The resistance of a metallic conductor is directly proportional to its length.

notes.front: How does a conductor’s cross-sectional area affect its resistance?
notes.back: Inversely: doubling the area halves the resistance.
notes.explanation: A larger area gives electrons more room to move without collision or capture by an atom.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Factors Affecting Resistance”, PDF p. 460
notes.evidence: If the cross-sectional area of a conductor is doubled, the resistance to current flow is reduced in half. This is true because of the increased area in which an electron can move without collision or capture by an atom.

notes.front: How does rising temperature affect the resistance of most conductor materials?
notes.back: Their resistance increases (carbon is an exception and decreases).
notes.explanation: A few alloys, such as constantan and Manganin, barely change, so the effect depends on the material.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Factors Affecting Resistance”, PDF p. 460
notes.evidence: Although some substances, such as carbon, show a decrease in resistance as the ambient (surrounding) temperature increases, most materials used as conductors increase in resistance as temperature increases.

notes.front: A wire run is replaced with one of the same gauge and material but three times as long. What happens to its resistance?
notes.back: A) It triples
notes.choices:
A) It triples
B) It falls to one-third
C) It stays the same
D) It rises ninefold
notes.choicesExplained: B) That would follow from a larger area, not a longer length. C) Length is one of the four properties that set resistance. D) Resistance is directly, not squarely, proportional to length.
notes.explanation: Resistance is directly proportional to length, so three times the length gives three times the resistance.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Factors Affecting Resistance”, PDF p. 459
notes.evidence: The longer the length of a given size of wire, the greater the resistance.

notes.front: What does a decrease of three wire gauge numbers do to the resistance of a given length of conductor?
notes.back: It cuts the resistance in half.
notes.explanation: Three gauge numbers roughly double the cross-sectional area, and resistance varies inversely with area.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Resistance and Relation to Wire Sizing”, PDF p. 461
notes.evidence: A decrease of three wire gauge numbers cuts the resistance of the conductor of a given length in half.

notes.front: A rectangular bus bar is 0.25 inch thick and 2 inches wide. What is its cross-sectional area in square mils?
notes.back: A) 500,000 square mils
notes.choices:
A) 500,000 square mils
B) 2,250 square mils
C) 0.5 square mils
D) 4,000,000 square mils
notes.choicesExplained: C) That multiplies the sides in inches and forgets to convert to mils. B) That adds the sides in mils instead of multiplying. D) That squares the width alone, a method for square conductors.
notes.explanation: Converting to mils gives 250 × 2,000, and the sides of a rectangle are multiplied.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Resistance and Relation to Wire Sizing”, PDF p. 461
notes.evidence: In the case of a rectangular conductor, the length of one side is multiplied by the length of the other.

notes.front: Which power formula uses only current and resistance?
notes.back: P = I²R.
notes.explanation: Substituting Ohm’s law (E = I × R) into P = I × E removes the voltage.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Power Formulas Used in the Study of Electricity”, PDF p. 463
notes.evidence: If we now substitute IR for E in the general formula, we get a formula that uses only current I and resistance R to determine the power in a circuit.

notes.front: Which power formula uses only voltage and resistance?
notes.back: P = E²/R.
notes.explanation: Substituting I = E/R into P = I × E removes the current.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Power Formulas Used in the Study of Electricity”, PDF p. 463
notes.evidence: we can again make a substitution such that power can be determined by knowing only the voltage (E) and resistance (R) of the circuit.

notes.front: A landing light draws 5 amperes from a 28-volt bus. What power does it use?
notes.back: A) 140 watts
notes.choices:
A) 140 watts
B) 33 watts
C) 5.6 watts
D) 0.18 watts
notes.choicesExplained: C) That divides voltage by current, which gives resistance, not power. B) That adds the values. D) That divides current by voltage.
notes.explanation: P = I × E, so 5 amperes times 28 volts is 140 watts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Power Formulas Used in the Study of Electricity”, PDF p. 463
notes.evidence: General Power Formula P = I (E) Where P = Power I = Current E = Volts

notes.front: A current of 3 amperes flows through a 10-ohm resistor. How much power does the resistor dissipate?
notes.back: D) 90 watts
notes.choices:
A) 30 watts
B) 3.3 watts
C) 300 watts
D) 90 watts
notes.choicesExplained: A) That is I × R, which is voltage, not power. C) That squares the resistance instead of the current. B) That divides R by I.
notes.explanation: With current and resistance known, power is current squared times resistance: 9 × 10.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–General (FAA-H-8083-30B, 2023), Chapter 12, “Power Formulas Used in the Study of Electricity”, PDF p. 463
notes.evidence: Second Form of Power Equation P = I2R

notes.front: How is total power found in a series or a parallel circuit?
notes.back: By adding the power dissipated in each resistor: `PT = P1 + P2 + P3 …`
